headline: The Ramayana push is easing: long-form fell to 5,408 views on 2026-11-12, its lowest day since 4 November, and breakouts still stand at 0 this month. Three decisions follow: the Ravana fact-check long-form by 19 November, a Tipu Sultan Short for 20 November, and the Guru Tegh Bahadur Short for 24 November.

top3.topic: Great Famine of 1876 to 1878: Wikipedia spike
top3.signal: English Wikipedia's page is at 4.79x its 30-day median; the pack does not show the cause. Itiha's Temple Short on the same famine has 1,169 views and failed for want of a picture.
top3.recommendation: Not one of the three decisions. Only if a slot opens: a Short on Lord Lytton's imperial assemblage of 1 January 1877, held while the famine ran, with Lytton named in sentence one. A pageview spike lasts days, so after 17 November drop it.

top3.signal: The same day as the Guru Tegh Bahadur moment. Itiha's Tarabai Short is one of the four breakouts. The date comes from the on-this-day feed, so it is lower confidence.
top3.recommendation: Second choice for 24 November, only after the Aurangzeb Short is recorded. Verify the date against a named source first.

top3.signal: “Why Is Lord Rama in the Original Constitution of India?” went up on 13 November with a like rate of 9.2% against a Shorts median of 3.9%.
top3.recommendation: Judge it on day three, 16 November. If it widens, a second Short on another illustration in the original document for 26 November.

more.topic: 4 December: “Maatrubhumi: May War Rest in Peace”, the next mass release
more.signal: Its trailer is the most-viewed history-matched video on YouTube India's chart this week. The radar lists it as a war film; the pack does not say which war. The T-14 step opens on 20 November.
more.recommendation: Find out by 20 November what it depicts. If it is a real event with a named antagonist, it becomes a decision next week: two Shorts scripted before release. Do not script from a trailer's framing.

skipped.topic: Children's Day, Nehru and the Gandhi-family spikes
skipped.signal: Nehru's Hindi Wikipedia page is at 23.84x its median and the hashtags lead X India, beside a row over a memoir.
skipped.source: X trends via getdaytrends, Wikipedia pageviews
skipped.recommendation: Skip. A calendar day and a party-political row; contemporary politics is a rejected species and a news spike is not evergreen demand.

whats_working: The best converter in the 90-day window is “How One Man Who Never Visited India Wrote Its History” at 12 net subscribers per 1,000: a named man convicted by his own record. Its verdict gives the shape for the Ravana long-form: “Name the villain, convict him with a document or payment he cannot deny, then end on who is still repeating him today.”

“Why Does All of Asia Know the Ramayana?” has crossed the hit line of 65 net subscribers and carried the long-form lever to 258 this month against 113 targeted. It is 41.8% of all long-form views over the 365-day window.

“Why Is Ram Setu Called ADAM'S Bridge?” is the best converter of the Ramayana-window Shorts, 1.2 per 1,000, and draws steady search every day. A title question answered with a dated map inside ten seconds is the search-side open to copy.
whats_wrong: Long-form reach is not becoming subscribers. The Asia video converts 2 net subscribers per 1,000 views and the Many Versions video 1.2. Part of that is the denominator: only 41.2% of November's long-form views were engaged views, so compare only with long-forms published since August, where these two are still among the three weakest. Probable cause: both open on a flat claim with no culprit on screen. Test: the Ravana long-form, culprit in sentence one, on the same film traffic.

Both Ramayana long-forms leak at the same seam, around 0:31 to 0:35, where the hook hands off to a tour or a chronology. The verdict that names it: “A map is not a hook; the viewer needs a person with a grievance.” Test: in the Ravana long-form the minute after the hook stays with the hook's person; compare the drop at that point.

Nothing made for the film window is built to convert. The four film Shorts convert between 0.2 and 0.6 net subscribers per 1,000, and the best-held converts worst, so retention is not the constraint. Probable cause: each answers one scene and ends. Test: the Tipu and Guru Tegh Bahadur Shorts told as complete stories at the longer length; compare per 1,000 on day three.

“Itihasa vs Myth” has 73 public views and “Is Caste Unique to India?” 244 twelve days on, with days of zero in Analytics after publish, while a third clip from the same conversation has 1,752 in three days. Probable cause: they were not public, or were restricted, at launch. Test: check both in Studio.

actions.action: Set the end screen and a pinned comment on both Ramayana long-forms to “How One Man Who Never Visited India Wrote Its History”.
actions.rationale: It takes minutes and works on traffic the channel already has; the library tail is behind at 15 against 42.

actions.action: Check “Itihasa vs Myth” and “Is Caste Unique to India?” in Studio for visibility history and restrictions.
actions.rationale: Days of zero views after publish suggest the first test never ran.

actions.action: Export Studio impressions and click-through for the two Ramayana long-forms.
actions.rationale: Click-through exists only in Studio exports.

growth.verdict: Needs 226 net subscribers a day. The channel does 31/day, so the target is a **7.3x** change in rate. Every lever this channel has demonstrated, pulled at once (scenario "4. Scenario 3 plus one breakout a quarter"), reaches 32.6/day — still 6.9x short. At that ceiling rate 100,000 arrives on 2033-10-23, 6.9 years out.

scenarios.name: 1. Current rate, nothing changes
assumptions: Measured: channel_totals_daily, everything the channel publishes, last 28 days.
Same formats, same cadence, same lane mix.
Includes the channel's one breakout: "Chakla: How the British Raj Created a ‘Licensed Vice’ System" is 1276 of the 2,813 subscribers that 21 fresh long-form videos produced.

scenarios.name: 2. Stop Shorts, same effort into long-form (no breakout)
assumptions: Carries the non-upload baseline of 12.5/day (350 of 806 net subscribers over 28 days came from no video). ASSUMPTION: it continues. It currently rests on one viral community post, so treat it as the least safe number here.
Measured: 21 long-form and 104 Shorts published in the last 365 days.
ASSUMPTION (not measured): 6 Shorts cost what 1 long-form costs, so the Shorts become 17.3 more long-form videos a year — 38.3 in total.
Measured: MEDIAN 32 subscribers per fresh long-form video. The mean is 134, inflated by one breakout, so the median is the honest number for planned output.
Gives up the 449 subscribers a year the Shorts brought in; they are simply absent from this total.
Below scenario 1 because scenario 1 contains a breakout and this one does not. That is the point, not an error.

scenarios.name: 3. All long-form, all revision lane (no breakout)
assumptions: Carries the non-upload baseline of 12.5/day (350 of 806 net subscribers over 28 days came from no video). ASSUMPTION: it continues. It currently rests on one viral community post, so treat it as the least safe number here.
Scenario 2's cadence, every topic chosen from the revision lane.
Measured on the same fresh set: 8 revision long-form videos, median 58 subscribers, against 32 for fresh long-form overall.
ASSUMPTION: the lane median holds as output scales. It rests on a small number of videos and is the weakest link here.

scenarios.name: 4. Scenario 3 plus one breakout a quarter
assumptions: Carries the non-upload baseline of 12.5/day (350 of 806 net subscribers over 28 days came from no video). ASSUMPTION: it continues. It currently rests on one viral community post, so treat it as the least safe number here.
Scenario 3, plus four videos a year performing like the best video the channel has ever published.
Measured: "Chakla: How the British Raj Created a ‘Licensed Vice’ System" brought 1,276 subscribers on 72,857 views.
ASSUMPTION: a breakout that size can be produced to order, four times a year. The channel has produced one.
